utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, sorry, could we go into private session for just one moment. The witness does not need to leave. I need to raise one matter. It's unrelated to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the Chamber move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Excellencies. Good afternoon to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I'd like to address you briefly, if I may. First of all, I hope I will -- you will have an understanding when I say that three witnesses a day are a lot to deal with even for a professional, let alone an amateur. Hence, I would like to ask for your permission not to have to examine the third witness and perhaps we could save some time in that regard. And if in any way possible, the time saved thus to be allocated to this witness. I also wanted to draw your attention to the fact that there are 500 paragraphs in this report, whereas I received 480 minutes for my examination. Even with simple yes or no answers, I'd still be unable to deal with them all. That is why I have to randomly choose the paragraphs and topics, since I have no other possibility. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In order to be clear, who do you refer to the third one?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Weren't we supposed to have a third witness in case we completed witness 039 in time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll consider that, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, I'll ask you only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber has decided to accommodate that request, which seems to be fair enough to the Chamber. So if you still keep him, you can release him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Further, we are going to have trial for five days next week. Very well. Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, I will only ask you about the foundation for your conclusions and I'll strive to put questions that can be answered with yes or no. In paragraph 2.73, you discuss the similarities and model of activity and conduct of the 1st Krajina Corps in the municipalities of the Krajina. Were you able to ascertain in which of those municipalities nothing happened and in which municipalities saw events that could not be compared to the model you propose?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in relation to disarmament operations that we've discussed in the last few days, I certainly saw similarities in the municipalities of Prijedor, Sanski Most, Novi, Kljuc, Kotor Varos, to a degree, although that happened a little bit later. There were movements out, I'm aware from the documents, in Banja Luka, although there was not the type of attacks that I saw in those other noted municipalities. One of the possible complications was that the zone of responsibility of the 1st Krajina Corps expanded and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Please only tell me whether you were able to observe how many municipalities there were where nothing happened and how many municipalities saw a mild model that you proposed. In other words, I'm trying to ask you whether the model was applied to all the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I was saying, one of the difficulties was that the corps expanded its zone of responsibility in the summer of 1992. So some of the municipalities in the corridor area were, I would argue, slightly different to those municipalities I've just mentioned. And that would seem to go back to the combat analysis readiness report, which indicated that there were, in essence, two phases: One phase where municipalities were secured, and then there was a second phase where larger operations took place. There were from the documents some municipalities where that pattern did not necessarily fit, possibly in --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's fine. How would it sound to you if I told you that a Muslim witness the other day told us that where they were, there were no problems where the Muslim population represented less than 50 per cent of the population, whereas problems occurred in such municipalities where they were accounted for, say one-half of the population, and he enumerated the municipalities where there were no problems at all.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In which municipality was this witness talking about, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, if you agree, in the Banja Luka Krajina there were 17 municipalities. If we add to that the municipalities of Derventa, Doboj, and those in the corridor, there was a total of over 20. In the initial group of 17 before the 1st Krajina Corps zone was expanded, was the model applied to all the municipalities, or did you make a calculation as to how many municipalities were absent of such events and how many municipalities saw a milder model applied to them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. No objection. If we could just -- not necessarily get a page cite, but a cite to the witness that Mr. Karadzic is referring to on the previous page at line 20. It can be told to me later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Yes, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether all 17 municipalities were in the zone of the 1st Krajina Corps. I would have to check on that. I did do a section on the area of responsibility of the 1st Krajina Corps. And I'm not sure what you mean by the issue of a milder model. What I do know is that in the municipalities I've articulated, they certainly seem to fit that model, of disarmament operations and taking control. It may well have been that in some of the other municipalities where the Serbs were a significant majority, that there was not the need to follow exactly that type of pattern. But even in municipalities, for example, in Celinac where the Muslims were I believe in a very small number, maybe even about 10 or certainly under 20 per cent, there are references in the 1st Krajina Corps of operations and attacks there, which we talked about before. So I -- it may well have been that some municipalities differed depending on their ethnicity, but there did seem a desire to control that -- those territories and municipalities in the ARK zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me remind you. In Celinac there were no operations. There were incidents, though, in the village of Bastasi. In some municipalities there were operations. Do you accept that there were operations only where they were armed Muslim forces, where they had initiated the killing of Serb soldiers deep in the rear of the Serb forces, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not agree with that characterisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I told you that 17 plus four or five municipalities in the corridor amounted to 22 or 23 municipalities which were within the zone of the corps and yet you can only enumerate four or five that fit your bill in the valley of the Sava, what would you say to that? Kljuc, Sanski Most, Prijedor, and Novi were in the Sana River valley which was one of the strategic goals to be achieved by the Muslim 5th Corps from Bihac. It was confirmed to us that this was so indeed by a Muslim witness. Do you accept or are you saying that wherever there was a larger concentration of Muslims, whatever the municipality, the Serbs attacked?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I wouldn't advocate that position, based on the documents I saw. This wasn't a report looking at every single municipality and every single known Serb populated area in that area. What I can say certainly in May and June the municipalities that I articulated and that were heavily reported in the documents of the 1st Krajina Corps did see these types of attacks and large numbers of individuals leaving the municipalities in the weeks and months following that. The corridor was a slightly different set of circumstances because the -- I believe mainly Croats had taken control of municipalities in the corridor from late March onwards in some of the municipalities. However, after operations by the 1st Krajina Corps had occurred in the summer of 1992, control was taken and I believe a large number of Croats in those municipalities fled. The situation in the corridor municipalities is slightly different, but it seems that the end result was quite similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that the Serbs were in the majority in Derventa, in Doboj, in Modrica, and they were not in the majority in Orasje and Odzak, and did you know that we managed to take Odzak back my peaceful means after the war?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that some of the municipalities in the corridor where Croats were in the majority or non-Serbs were in the majority and in some municipalities that Serbs were in the municipality -- Doboj, for example, was one that was not a Serb majority and there were a number of other ones as well. So it's not an area that I studied and the ethnic break-up of -- the ethnic make-up of the municipalities in Doboj -- sorry, in the corridor was not an area of this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether you answered the question, Mr. Brown. The question was: Did you know that we managed -- Mr. Karadzic, we managed to take Odzak back by peaceful means after the war.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure what Mr. Karadzic means by peaceful means or whether as part of the Dayton Agreement Odzak was to be returned back to RS control and placed in the territory of the RS. It may well have been because it might have been a Serbian -- predominantly Serbian municipality. It may well have been that it was part of the Dayton Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I may have misspoken or there may have been a misinterpretation. We controlled Odzak and Croats were in the majority there before the war. After the war we returned it to the Croats.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karadzic, that may well have been the case. I know that Serb VRS forces, 1 Krajina Corps forces took control of the territory in the summer, but it may well have been as part of the Dayton Agreement and that was returned to Croat or non-Serb control. But I would imagine it was part of the Dayton Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please look at -- sorry, of course as a soldier you will agree that one does not return territory before a peace agreement is concluded; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's a rather general question which I'm not sure I can answer one way or the other. Territory can be returned for military purposes, but clearly territory can be returned as part of negotiated settlements. Territory can be returned to control of peacekeepers or buffer zones. I'm not sure what you -- what you exactly mean. There's no simple answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please look at 2.88 and 2.89. In 2.89, you say that it is obvious that Major-General Talic did very little, save for submitting a report about an incident in two combat reports of his. I wouldn't call the event in question an incident, but rather a tragedy, a crime, which occurred at Mount Vlasic. And this is what you refer to in that paragraph. In your view, Talic should have done more; is that correct? It's paragraph 2.89.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I potentially think General Talic should have done more. I'm not saying that he didn't do anything because he reported up his chain, but it seemed to me that he was certainly emphasising the fact that no soldiers were involved in it. There could have been, I would have thought, a significant amount more that General Talic could have done. But I'm not saying that he didn't do anything because he did report up the chain and clearly the events involved or the perpetrators identified in the Krajina Corps documents identify the police as the perpetrators. And I would certainly agree with your characterisation that -- well, a tragedy and it was clearly a very significant incident in which a large number of people were killed on Mount Vlasic and thrown down the canyon. Bearing in mind the gravity of the incident, I would have thought General Talic may well have done a lot more than just report it up his chain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that General Talic, like Colonel Peulic, investigated whether the military was involved and their conclusion was that it was not; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: From his statement in the media, he indicates that the army carried out an investigation into whether members were involved and claims that they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that the military was not competent to deal with the civilian police and that there was nothing for him to do, save for reporting it to his superiors?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can only say as a former soldier and as -- and reading the documents that, yes, he did report it up the chain. But I would argue that he could have done more than that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, in your opinion, what could or should he have done more, other than reporting it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe he could have secured the site. I could have -- he could well have conducted a thorough investigation on his own to find out exactly who did it and under what circumstances. He could well have used his own investigative military police resources to conduct a very thorough investigation, and then pass that on to the civilian authorities in order to be part of a wider investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Having found that the perpetrators were police members, do you say that he had the jurisdiction to investigate into police members?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the legislation necessarily, but he clearly knows who the perpetrators are very quickly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And Colonel Peulic was the operations group commander of that zone. In essence, it was a military zone. And I believe also that the -- you know, the convoy was going through the operation group commander's zone, an area. So the military were not completely and utterly out of it, but it's clear that the perpetrators are identified as the police. I'm not sure what the legal -- the legal laws for General Talic would be in terms of prosecuting the police. I doubt that very much. However, bearing in mind the large numbers of people that were involved in this and the instantaneously knowledge that General Talic had that the event had occurred, I think I put in my report he probably did the bare minimum. But I do think that he probably could have done more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, in paragraph 2.88, we can see what Peulic proposed. Did you know that his unit did secure the scene, and did you know that the civilian police as well as the Ministry of Defence and the CSB immediately took part in investigations and that Talic had nothing to do there?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. In paragraph 2.140, you discuss the policy of moving people out. Did you come across my messages, Telefax messages, by which I prohibited that civilians be moved?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not evident to me in the documents that I reviewed, Mr. Karadzic, and if you would like to show them I'm sure I can read them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I can show one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it please be 65 ter 1397. 65 ter 13937. This is not it. Yes, this is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I will read until we manage to establish whether there is a translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Karadzic be asked to read very slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, could you repeat. Start again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Title: "Office of the State Security Service Mrkonjic Grad." The body of the document: "We forward in its entirety a dispatch of the RDB in Sarajevo III," that is to say the 3rd Administration and we have the number, which has to do with the moving out of civilians from the municipality of Srbobran. This was our name for Gornji Vakuf. There they go on to quote the entire message: "We forward the entire information note about the moving out of civilians from the area of Srbobran municipality which was sent to the president of the RS, Mr. Radovan Karadzic, by the president of the Municipal Assembly, Srbobran Nedeljko Ninkovic, and an MP at the National Assembly of the RS Nikola Kisin." Third paragraph: "President, we informed you about the removal of population from this area at an earlier stage," we have the date, "following which we received your order," we have the number, "about the prohibition of removing people from our area. We are abiding by it strictly. We orally informed you that the chief of the SJB in Srbobran was trying to talk people into moving out and he admitted to having done so in the CSB in Banja Luka before" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter missed the last sentence because the page was scrolled down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, could you start again from the part interpreters couldn't follow.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "We acquainted the commander of the 30th Division, Colonel Zec, about the removal and who was doing it. Since then, things have not become any better. Basically, the entire area of Turbet and Golos have been moved out from. There are still individual cases of people moving from the area of Srbobran and certain permits were issued to that effect by the command of the 19th Light Infantry Brigade and commander Lieutenant-Colonel Ljubomir Jekic and Mr. Kovacevic. We also have information confirming that such certificates were issued by the SJB in Srbobran, although they are not registered anywhere. Although there is a mixed check-point by the military and civilian police in two and a half years, very few people were returned with personal effects. They are all basically dragging their feet. We tried to warn them but it is of no use. It is necessary to expand on the information received and to forward them a.s.a.p. to this administration." So this refers to the area from Srbobran to Mrkonjic Grad, and then it was reported to Banja Luka and Sarajevo having finally reached me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you come across this document. Can you see that for two and a half years there were attempts to prevent such occurrences, and could you see here that people themselves were asking for certificates, for permits to move out, whereas we were trying to prevent them from receiving them?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only go on the translation there. It's not clear to me whether they're talking about Serbs who are in Srbobran who want to get away from the conflict zone, which I believe Srbobran and Donji Vakuf were right on the front line. It may well have been that the people we're talking about here are Serbs who might want to move to a safer location or it may well be that it's non-Serbs. It's not clear to me. I'm not sure in 1994 the ethnic make-up of Srbobran municipality was, but I do know that it was, in essence -- as far as I'm aware, it was made up predominantly of Serb areas of the wider Donji Vakuf municipality that had existed before the conflict. So I would have to read the document again and it may well be that what they're saying here is that we don't want Serbs to leave this area and they might be wanting to leave because of the conflict zone that was going on there because it becomes a territory that we're not populating. It may well be that they're talking about the last remnants or the remnants of non-Serbs who are in Srbobran who want to move to Central Bosnia. I'm not clear from the document. Also the date is of some note, I think you're talking about 1994 here and it may well be a specific -- specific issue related to this area. But it seems to be, you know, two years after 1992 in which my report covers, where large numbers of non-Serbs, significantly number of non-Serbs, had left a number of Krajina municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But here you see it doesn't state the ethnicity of these persons. This is about civilians and it says that -- it refers to two and a half years, which means that all of 1992 is included. However, in your paragraph 148 you say that in the 1st Krajina Corps they're reporting that in the zone of responsibility there is a special problem is -- posed by Muslims and Croats who are seeking permission to move out of the area in which they live and move to territories held by the forces of the zone at Beretke and HVO. And then the Red Cross in Mrkonjic Grad is negotiating what the HVO from Jajce and the authorities from neighbouring municipalities are trying to reach agreement. So can you see that this is about from the Muslims from Donji Vakuf which is the same as Srbobran and that in all the municipalities on both sides of the line of conflict there are efforts made to let the population cross the line?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you seem to be characterising the movement in 1992 as somehow this voluntarily movement. And it's, I think -- from the documents I've highlighted and some of the references in the report, I don't see that. When we look at the issue of the ARK decisions, references in the 1st Krajina Corps that we must strive for complete separation, when we look at references in the 1st Krajina Corps that people are not going to be allowed to return, when we look at documents, for example, the Novi documents, large number of people were leaving and I don't believe -- I don't see it as a voluntarily, happy movement out of the territory. These were large numbers of people in a very short space of time, it seems to me from the documents I have reviewed, who were moving and being forced to move out of territory that is wanted to be controlled by the RS authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll get there yet.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Has it been notified to the Prosecution? I didn't see this in the list.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm not sure, Your Honour, but in any event no objection, pending translation, from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D1939, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, please take into consideration that during the war we called Donji Vakuf Srbobran. So it's one and the same place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, Mr. Brown, can you see here to 2.141. You are citing a document that speaks about the HVO from Jajce negotiating with the Red Cross of Mrkonjic Grad for the Serbs from Jajce to be taken to the other side and the Croats and Muslims from Mrkonjic Grad in the opposite direction. And it says on the principle of allowing people to choose freely where they will live, if this change is effected successfully, it will be followed by an exchange of prisoners of war. This is what you stated here, isn't it? You cite this document.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What footnote is that, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 538, the regular combat report of the 1st Krajina Corps dated 13 August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just to answer Your Honour's last question, it was not notified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And untranslated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Additional information I'm missing that doc. Came in. [Interpretation] I think it's arrived. We should check the e-mail.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would seem to be what the document says. There were references and there were, indeed, Red Cross agreements. Whether these people are voluntarily moving is another question. And just I think for clarification, I don't think Srbobran covered the whole of Donji Vakuf. As I'm aware, Srbobran was only the small part of Donji Vakuf municipality. It wasn't -- it wasn't the whole municipality. I believe it was just the part that the RS territory controlled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: For your information, all of Srbobran was remained Donji Vakuf and the Serb controlled all of Srbobran until autumn 1995, but never mind. Mr. Brown, now we can make conjectures one way or the other, but you made an analysis based on documents. This document speaks about the wishes of the two parties and the negotiations that took place to enable people to move to a zone where they felt safer. Now, when you say we don't know if it's voluntarily, that's another question. What I'm asking you is: Are you confusing voluntarily movements and movement due to fear, being made to move? Now, what exactly do you mean? Fleeing before the police or other forces or driving people out through fear? Do you distinguish there?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honours, if we're talking about footnote 538 still that's 04204 is the 65 ter number if Mr. Karadzic wishes to call it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And further I note that item was included in the e-mail.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Oh, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think I'm confused -- I'm confusing. Clearly there are -- may be many reasons why individuals do want to move, and one of them could well be that in their combat zones they're -- they are frightened. I don't doubt that for a minute. There are many other reasons. For example, in one of the combat reports on the 30th or 31st, I believe, of May, after operations in Kljuc, Kozarac, Sanski Most, which they specifically refer, they make reference to the fact that conscripts of a Muslim ethnicity are asking to leave the Krajina Corps and the reason that they're doing that is because they -- they are unhappy about the massive destruction of their towns in those areas. And that's a combat report of the corps. So the destruction that was occurring in these attacks undoubtedly led to significant fear, but I go back to my point that the ARK Crisis Staff was issuing instructions that the military were interpreting that people were going to be leaving the area in large numbers and would not be returning. And that those leaving, that they were going to be expecting Serbs in other territory to come into RS territory. And so, yes, undoubtedly many people probably were frightened and fled and wanted to leave, but this issue of forcible movement is clearly evident in the documents and it would seem to me that the military and the 1st Krajina Corps in particular were aware that there was a forcible removal of individuals and that people, once they had left, were not going to be coming back. And also in the police documents with issues such as deregistration, permanent deregistration documents being signed, it would seem to me that reading those documents that a large number of people were not voluntarily moving, but they were moving and they would not come back to their homes, whether their homes existed in some cases or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, I don't have time to clarify this. I put it to you that the organised forces, that is, the army and the police, moved nobody forcibly. I'll try to prove that in other words. But do you think that a decision made by a municipality that someone may not return is valid? Isn't the RS the negotiating party and that with regard to return, only the RS has a say and only that -- only their decisions are valid?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is your point that someone can stay only if the RS authorises them to stay? Is that your point, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm speaking about the right of refugees to return. Have you seen the documents in which I say that refugees and abandoned property are a temporary occurrence and that after the war everything must be restored and everybody must be given the right to return. Have you come across any such document of mine which also presupposes the ban of influencing anybody's decision whether or not to move?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The documents I reviewed in the Krajina Corps and select -- other documents in relation to the ARK, I didn't see that, Mr. Karadzic, I didn't that at all. And all I can say is from the documents that I see, some of the military documents would seem to indicate there was an understanding in their own documents that individuals who were leaving were not going to be returning and that there was a desire to have Serbs in other territories come to RS territory. And, in essence, that that would have -- that that was a policy certainly pushed out through the ARK.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And have you seen that whoever wrote that nonsense also said that Serbs, too, who didn't want to take part in combat were also leaving the RS and that they also would not be allowed to return?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may well have said that in that document. I would have to go back to it again. It wouldn't surprise me. I think there may well have been a belief that people that were trying to not take part in this or not become part of the RS military and maybe who fled to Serbia were somehow traitors or not supporting the cause. It may well have been that that's what was echoed in those documents. It may well have been that a significant number of Serbs in the RS didn't support the policy and I wonder if that was one of the reasons they may well have left. But I don't doubt it that that type of comment may well have appeared in some of the Krajina Corps military documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you didn't only read military documents, but also the -- those of the Crisis Staff of the AR Krajina, which stated that Serbs, not only Muslims, who were leaving the RS would also lose some of their rights. You may have seen in some documents that both Serbs and Muslims leaving the RS would lose some rights?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That may well have been the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that on 19 August I made null and void all certificates about the surrender of property? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, no -- just for the record, could we get the year?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1992. Through Witness Doyle, we tendered the document. He informed me on 16 August in London about this occurrence and immediately upon returning to Pale on 19 August, I ordered -- I made an order to declare all this null and void and he told me chapeau, he didn't know that I had done that. I'm not sure under which number it was admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that as of 22 April 1992 I advocated, among others, the right of refugees to return in all documents and that I signed many documents stating that this was their unalienable right, that is, either the return of refugees or their compensation for the property lost or destroyed during the war? D1754 is the document number, the one of 19 August 1992.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karadzic, I'm not aware of the instruction on the 22nd of April. All I can say is that whatever instruction you passed out on that day did not seem to have an effect on the Krajina some months later, if, indeed, that's -- was a genuine attempt.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Brown, I don't expect a witness to be as biassed as to doubt the documents issued by the president of a republic, documents that have been issued. Do leave these things to the Prosecution. But did you see any documents and were you aware of the actions of the leadership of the state? That was my interest. But now I know that you did not see any such documents. Now I will move on to paragraph 2.134, although thousands of non-Serbs ended in detention centres before being removed from the Krajina area, it is evident that larger numbers of Muslims and Croats either fled, were forced and expelled their homes or were desperate enough to leave. Do you consider it important enough for this Trial Chamber to draw a distinction between these reasons, for the Trial Chamber to know who fled, who was expelled, and what number of people were desperate enough to leave? For the purpose of criminal proceedings, these distinctions matter.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I don't really think I'm in a position to explain or advise the Trial Chamber of the importance of their work and job.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you think that it's all of the same weight, all these reasons I mean, or that difference is significant and that it should be pointed out?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a lawyer and -- Mr. Karadzic, and I'm not presenting that in a way that has legal weight. My analysis leads me to the conclusion, as I've talked about before, that there was a desire to mark out RS territory through articulation such as the 16th Assembly Session, although not exclusively that, there was an articulation to map out territory that you and others in the RS leadership wanted to control and that part of that would involve the moving out of large numbers of people who were viewed as being against RS -- the RS state. Whether individuals were all forced out or felt frightened enough to leave or took up offers of the Red Cross and other humanitarian organisations to leave or through massive destructions of property and their own homes felt desperate enough to leave, to me is all part of the same issue. My analysis of documents that I saw lead me to the conclusion that there was a desire to mark out RS territory and to ensure that within that RS territory there would not be a large number of individuals who were viewed as enemies, and were viewed as against that state, and that's what I -- and how they left, it was not part of the detail of this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Nicholls, the exhibit Mr. Karadzic referred to as his order to comply with Geneva Conventions or something like that is D1754 is still under seal. Is it for the same reason as you referred to yesterday and being still the subject of further consideration?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It may be -- it may be, Your Honours. As I said, though, we did file a chart and my recollection is all those types of materials Mr. Karadzic, his orders to obey the Geneva Conventions, and those types of things, we did not mark to be under seal on our chart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, one thing is marking the borders of the RS, and I put it to you that all three parties agreed to these borders as well as the fourth party, the European Community, which offered. If you're not familiar with the conference, then say so, but when you speak about the borders, I put it to you that that was exactly how it was. Do you know that the borders in existence have been accepted by all four sides?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said to you before, I do not believe the discussions about borders in and around the Cutileiro discussions are exactly the same as the borders that the RS state articulated as they wanted to have through discussions before and in particular at the 16th Assembly Session. I think there are differences in those borders. If you're talking about the existence of borders now and the borders that were established in Dayton, there are differences between Dayton and RS territory, as articulated in 1992. But it is not a significant or detailed area of my report. The borders are important but not the differences between the various negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I won't ask you whether or not in negotiations you start with the lowest price or start high and then negotiate. But where did you get the information that can also be found in the document that we wanted to separate ourselves from the Muslims who also stayed in the RS, when it says the separation of states belonging to the other two peoples? Did you take that from the indictment or was that section of the indictment taken from you? And how does that match your thesis that there was no removal in some municipalities, there were some villages such as Janja near Bijeljina and others where nobody left?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I've been trying not to object. That is an extremely large, compound question, and it's up to Mr. Karadzic -- but a lot of that ground was gone over on the first day. It's up to him if he wants to go over it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Karadzic, you can reformulate your question in a simpler form.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Brown, that there is no place in the RS in which there were no Muslims left until the end of the war, except possibly for Drvar, but there were no Muslims there even before the war? There is no one settlement where a significant number of Muslims did not stay until the war. I mean, that's a simple question.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may well be that there were numbers of Muslims that did remain in a number of areas. I'm not stating in my report that every single Muslim in RS territory was to be expelled. I think in your own words at the 16th Assembly Session, you indicated: We do not want large numbers. So I'm not advocating that there may well have been some pockets of non-Serbs that remained in RS territory, maybe even through the whole war. But I stick to my assertion that through the documents that I saw, there was an expectation that large numbers of non-Serbs in RS territories would not remain in RS territory. You, yourself, I believe, on one of the Deputy Club meetings in February indicated that you wanted 90 per cent of Serbs in your republic and that that may mean that 10 per cent were outside, but that we would make space for them, we would have them if necessary. So I don't argue that at the 16th Assembly Session this was the first time they were talking about separation, nor that every single Muslim in RS territory was going to necessarily leave but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you --

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I do assert that in the establishment of the RS, large numbers and significantly large numbers were not expected to stay and, in fact, were moved out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, first of all, your calculation that 90 per cent of the Serbs should be in the RS doesn't mean that only 10 per cent remained elsewhere, but that around 90 per cent of the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina with their territories should join the RS. But you also saw that I opposed territorial megalomania, which means we did not covet territories that were not ours, because otherwise we would have had a large number of persons who were dissatisfied with the RS. And you still claim that I meant people who stayed in the RS, and, secondly, that 90 per cent of the overall population of the RS were Serbs, none of which is correct. You misunderstand it totally. Me, Izetbegovic, and Boban agreed that every village, if possible --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are not to argue with the witness. You are supposed to put a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question is: Were you saying that it was our wish for 90 per cent of the population of the RS to be of Serbian ethnicity, or that we wanted 90 per cent of all Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina to live in our territorial unit; the former or the latter?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to go over the Deputy Club minutes, but it's my understanding that you articulated then that 90 per cent of Serbs in Bosnia should be within RS territory. And that along with some other references in other minutes and, importantly, the 16th Assembly Session, leads me to the conclusion that in RS territory there was going to be predominantly Serb, large numbers of non-Serbs would not be welcome in RS territory, and events and the days and weeks after the 16th Assembly Session --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- seemed to indicate that large numbers did not remain and were forcibly removed from that territory and, in fact, had already occurred in a number of municipalities even prior to the 16th Assembly Session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you get to see my speech of the 25th of January, 1992, in the joint Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, where I said: If you proclaim independence and if you go for a referendum, before regionalisation a war is going to break out, everybody is going to kill everybody else, everybody is going to flee to their own areas, we will become homogenous, and yet again we will have to seek agreement? Have you seen that speech at all? Did you take it into account at all?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see that speech, Mr. Karadzic. It may well be that that's what you said in the Assembly session. Concurrent with that, I think, the SDS leadership as I've articulated through some JNA documents were certainly arming and preparing that if negotiations failed that territory was going to be seized and that that territory was going to consist predominantly of Serb-controlled municipalities and that large numbers of non-Serbs in those municipalities would be removed. And I believe certainly in some of the ARK municipalities I saw, that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, I reject that as strongly as possible and claim that you do not have any support in anything to be claiming that. Let us now look at --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not catch the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the 24th of April, the corps together with government organs, state organs, tried to prevent attacks and the forcible removal of people [In English] "In co-operation with the governmental organs to prevent attacks and they forced eviction of people regardless of their ethnic or religious background." [Interpretation] So it's the army --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, what are we talking about? Could you give the number again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2.135, paragraph 2.135, and this is Mr. Brown's very own findings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that the corps were telling on themselves, or is it not clear that the government and the corps were against that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I argue in the report that certainly in the periods of March and April the JNA did pass down some instructions which indicated that they wished to try and defuse ethnic tensions and that they wanted to try and prevent attacks in areas. I believe this was probably to try and keep Bosnia within Yugoslavia. After all, they were a federal --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, you're reading things into this. Is it not clear here that the authorities and the army are against this? You are reading your very own thoughts into this. I'm asking you what you actually found here. Did you write here that it was clear in April that the government and the authorities were trying to prevent undesirable things from happening?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do not, please, interrupt the witness with his answer. Please continue, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it is part of this twin-track policy. The JNA, I believe, were trying to keep as much of Yugoslavia together. They did pass down instructions that indicated that they wished to try and defuse ethnic tensions, some instructions, and I think this reference is someone of them. Concurrently with that, they were also -- there were also references that they clearly sided with the Serb position, that they were disseminating and distributing weapons, and also even before this date, that they had assisted in operations in certain municipalities which involved Serb organs taking control. So I believe, yes, there was references of which this is one, that they wished to try and preserve some degree of harmony. But I also think that concurrent with that there were -- there were examples where they were assisting, for example, in Zvornik in operations that resulted in the take-over of those municipalities, Krupa being another one, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was Zvornik your task --

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Excellency, I cannot have him recounting his own findings to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Hear him out and then you can ask the question. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hope I've made my point there, Your Honour. I think there was this twin-track policy and, in fact, I don't deny that there were JNA references, in fact I quote some of them about this desire to reduce tensions. And it also came at a time when the JNA themselves were a bit unclear as to what was going to happen to them, at least formally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, you say further on in this paragraph is -- is that the people were afraid, panic-stricken, and that they were already leaving certain territories. And you say further on: [In English] "The 1st Krajina Corps reported that the population were fearful and apprehensive and that pressure to move out from these areas was growing." [Interpretation] Did you locate where this pressure was coming from?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. This was a reference from the 1st Krajina Corps. It may well have been the statement you made earlier on -- could have been one of them -- one of the types of statements that were adding to the pressure along with others, not just yourself. But I'm sure that there were many statements going around that certainly added to the tensions, both locally and at a high level. But I didn't look into the details. All I'm doing is reporting what the Krajina Corps put in their daily combat reports, that tension was rising, people were fearful, and it was clear that they were apprehensive maybe in what had happened in some municipalities in other places, that they were -- that they were fearful about what was going to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You see, in the footnote here, 520, you rely on document 9417, so let us have a look at that. Let us see page 3 in e-court, otherwise it's page 2 in the document itself. 9417, that's the 65 ter number. While we're waiting for that, Mr. Brown, this is what I'm saying to you, that they are reporting that the pressure to have people moved out comes from the persons who actually want to move out and to change their residence. Did you understand that? It's not that somebody else is exerting pressure against them to move out; they are seeking this themselves, as we saw in the telegram a moment ago, they're asking to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 2, please, of this document -- in e-court it's 3 actually. Because there is a empty one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you answer that? Did you notice that this pressure for moving out came from those who wanted to move out?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't read it like that, Mr. Karadzic. People presumably were moving out because they were frightened, and for people to move out of their homes and even contemplate the issue of moving out of their homes, there presumably must have been a significant threat to them. This document comes already after certain municipalities had been taken over. For example, Prijedor on the 30th of April, this comes a week after that. It comes a week or a few days after artillery was moved into Prijedor. And incidents were happening, and it may well have been that what was going on and what they expected and what they felt was going to happen in those areas led them to be fearful and led them to contemplate moving out of their areas. And they may well have been aware of what happened in Krupa and what had happened in other parts of Bosnia such as --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, sir, it's not for you to say maybe. Your report is full of maybes. I am asking you whether you see what it says here, the population is fearful, panic-stricken, there is a great deal of emigration to other parts of the country, I don't think that this has been translated properly. It says many people are fleeing. The original says there is a great deal of emigration within the country, people going to other parts of the country, regardless of the moral and political aspect of why people are fleeing from their homes I want to make this distinction for this Trial Chamber whether somebody comes to other people's homes telling them to leave or whether people are trying to leave out of fear. I, as the Defence here, need to make this distinction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Karadzic, you're spending a lot of your time making comment. If you need to make a distinction, you must turn it into a proper question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just briefly, Your Honours, I object to Mr. Karadzic yelling at the witness: "Sir, sir, it's not for you to say maybe ..." The witness is trying to answer questions posed to him and I think is doing his best -- well, I'll just cut it at that. He shouldn't tell the witness what words he's allowed to use in his answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. What is your question? I think you are coming to a close, but ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document please be admitted? If I'm getting close to the end, I'm saying that this witness has not been cross-examined. Out of 12 topics, I've done -- I've dealt with only one. Could this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1940, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask the Trial Chamber whether I can offer all the documents mentioned by this witness in his report through a bar table motion, the documents that have not been tendered by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I would have no objection to that, Your Honours. It might be useful in your review of the report. And as I said earlier, I would -- plan to discuss with Mr. Robinson but I haven't, but we have a hyperlinked chart of all of the footnotes, which also has the 65 ter numbers, so that if you have the report open and you're next to your computer, you can click on the footnote and read the document. And we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I was just going to say, it could take us a bit of time, but we could also, because we've done that in the past, hyperlink the actual report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, how does it fit to a bar table motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, we -- to comply with your requirements for a bar table motion, we should demonstrate how each of the documents are relevant and how they fit into our case. I have to say that as Defence counsel I seriously question the wisdom of offering all of the exhibits of this witness. I can see why the Prosecution would want to do that. I really can't see why the Defence would want to do that, but perhaps that's something we could discuss between myself and Dr. Karadzic, and if a bar table motion is appropriate we can make one in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I note the time, Mr. Karadzic. How much more would you need to conclude your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, of course I'd need another two days at least, but can I have at least one hour to give one example per topic at least? Because there are many topics here, 10 or 12 of them, and I didn't have enough time to deal with any of them. As for documents, I don't want to tender everything. I want to tender what the witness mentioned, what the witness relied upon, and what the OTP did not tender. I would like to make a selection out of those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will take a break now for 25 minutes, and then, Mr. Karadzic, you will have half an hour to conclude, just that. We will resume at five past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, you've just mentioned me as the author of certain ideas that you refer to as criminal and that have to do with these movements. Actually, I have to find this other thing now, the relations between the centre of Republika Srpska, Pale, and the RK Krajina. For example, in paragraph 1.113 on page 50 did you mention all your references on the basis of which you created this paragraph, as it were, 185, 186, 187?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You ask a question one at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I've heralded the topic as such and now I'm asking about the paragraph. Did you create this paragraph on the basis of the documents mentioned in these three footnotes or is there something else that you have not mentioned?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a long time since the wrote the report, Mr. Karadzic. I'm not sure if there were other references, but these are the references I've cited.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you thought it was sufficient to quote a newspaper article from "Kozarski Vjesnik" and two reports of the 1st Corps; right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the documents were cited, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 1.114 you also speak of the Crisis Staff and you mention two sources, 188 and 189, those are the footnote numbers; right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you think that that was sufficient for you, to have an overall insight into the work of the Crisis Staff and its links with the army?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The report wasn't written in order to have an insight into the work of the ARK Crisis Staff. This section was part of a wider section that I believed that the ARK, like at municipal level in the Krajina there was a relationship, a close relationship, between the military and the civilian authorities. And also that the police were represented usually as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at the next paragraph, 1.115. This is what you say: [In English] "There was a concerted effort by the 1st Krajina Corps to establish and maintain links with the civilian authorities at all levels. On the 7th of May, 1992, some weeks prior to many of the military attacks in the Krajina municipalities, a meeting was held concerning the future status of the JNA involving both military commanders of the corps and the civilian authorities." [Interpretation] So you considered this to be something undesirable or something that is proof of a crime, the fact that the army and the civilian authorities were in contact; right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't make the assertion of either. The reason I added this in - and there are many other documents too - was that it seemed to me that the military and the civilian authorities did work closely together and that that happened at the senior level with General Talic but it also happened significantly at the lower level with his brigades and subordinate brigades and there were other documents or a few documents, actually, that I think add to that assertion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us look at 1.105 and from 118 to 119, where you talk about the relationship between the government and -- or rather, Prime Minister Djeric and the instructions on the work of the Crisis Staffs of Serb people in the municipalities. I don't need to read it out, so what you mention there are the first three paragraphs; right? And then in paragraph 1.107 you say: [In English] "An important factor in the implementation of the overall policies of the SDS and the functioning of the self-proclaimed Bosnian Serb organs on the ground." [Interpretation] And you link this to a common purpose, and so on and so forth. So you think that Crisis Staffs are an example of how SDS policy was pursued and that Branko Djeric's instruction is a telling example of that; right? P3439, that's the number of this document otherwise.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do think the Crisis Staffs were an important body and that they brought together the military and police and the civilian organs, certainly at local level. And I think there is documentation that would highlight that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, on the basis of this paragraph you claim that they were supposed to carry out instructions from the central levels of government; right? And that's the purpose of these instructions; right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that there is enough documentation to show that the Crisis Staffs responded to tiers above municipality. And I think if you take, for example, the issue -- one of the municipalities like Sanski Most, which the documentation is quite significant, you can see the documentation flows down to the Crisis Staff, decisions are taken at the Crisis Staff certainly in relation to disarmament operations, those are passed on, there are decisions taken in order to -- for example, in Sanski Most for Colonel Andzic and Colonel Basara to conduct operations. We saw the document yesterday or previously --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm just asking you to stick to the document, Djeric's document that you referred to. You mentioned this document as an example of the link between the central organs and the municipalities; right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It's not the only one. I think the Subotic instruction is also another example. And I'm not saying these are the only mechanisms. Certainly when the army was established, there seems to be meetings at the senior level, directives used. So I'm not saying it is the only one but I do think the Crisis Staffs -- and in fact, the combat analysis readiness report makes specific reference to that, the importance of Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, why then did you omit paragraphs 9, 10, and 13? Why didn't you draw the attention of the Trial Chamber to that? P34359, we haven't got much time, but let's have that called up and let's have a look at this, 9, 10, and 13. It require the municipal authorities to do certain things that you omitted to mention to the Trial Chamber. Is that because you worked for the OTP? Is that fair towards the Defence and towards the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I see what paragraphs 9, 10, and 13 are?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll upload -- let us upload it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Towards the bottom we have item 9 in the English and in the Serbian as well, I believe. The original states that the Crisis Staff is under an obligation to create working conditions for the international peace and relief organisations and to ensure an unimpeded transport of relief convoys to their destinations. Perhaps "shall provide" may be slightly confusing. [In English] Translation. [Interpretation] Could we have the next page in English so as to be able to see item 10: "The non-fighting population and the wounded must be treated in the most humane fashion and in accordance with the ICRC. Prisoners of war also must be treated humanely and in accordance with the laws of the Serbian Republic of BiH."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps omit to draw the Chamber's attention to it as part of your discussion of this document?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I referred in the report itself that the document wasn't -- also my report wasn't a study in all components and actions of the Crisis Staff and that the reference to the Djeric instruction was more of a general one, making the point that Crisis Staffs existed and that they were to involve the issue of the military working in co-operation with the civilian authorities. I didn't omit that. On reflection I might well have included certainly number 10. I might well have put that in a section either quoted there or I might even have included it later on in the report when we're talking about issues relating to prisoners of war, for example, when General Talic issued his own instructions of prisoners of war. Maybe that's an omission on my part, but I don't think I was using the document particularly to forensically examine every aspect of the operation of Crisis Staffs. It was more a general point. There was others that were looking at Crisis Staffs in more detail than I was. It was used in relation to identifying the Crisis Staffs that existed, that the militaries were to be a component of that, and, in fact, I would argue were a significant feature certainly in that first phase that the combat analysis readiness report discusses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In any case, paragraph 1.105 contains part of this document and the paragraphs referred to are not mentioned or commented upon; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The references are part of the document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Next you conclude that it was the policy of the top political leadership was disseminated to lower levels and look at 1.118 of your report. There you seem to suggest quite the opposite. It is paragraph 1.118: [In English] "Notwithstanding all the positive tendencies in the Bosnian Krajina are its leadership in its public statements and concrete political actions maintain an independent attitude toward the SR BH government and there are attempts to interfere in commanding the corps and some of its structures." [Interpretation] This document is dated the 14th of June, correct, and you took note of it; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 1.119, you discuss a political struggle between Banja Luka and the Pale government which was evident in the summer months of 1992. It goes on to say that: "... certain manifestations of which were reflected within the military reports at the time." Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is a small number of references and I thought they were important enough to put in my analysis. There weren't that many, however, and there were meetings, at least references to meetings that General Talic took part in, in order to try and resolve some of those differences. So I hope that I'm up front in the report in presenting that there was this issue. I do not see, however, that as somehow being so serious that the Krajina Corps was unable to function or the Krajina Corps was stopped in carrying out the tasks that it did. But the report does make reference to the fact that there were -- there are -- there seem to be tensions at times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In any case, you noted that the Krajina was quite isolated until September 1992 and that the corridor was unsafe. It wasn't made safe until early July and that the telephone network functioned poorly; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe the last point. I'm not sure when you say the telephone network functioned poorly, I don't think that happened. Certainly the combat analysis readiness report doesn't say that. They certainly utilised the telephone very much as a means when other military means were not functioning. So I would disagree with you there. I wouldn't argue that the Krajina was necessarily isolated until September 1992 at all. It is my understanding that the corridor was taken or some of the municipalities were taken over in March, late March I believe, which in essence meant that road through the Krajina towards Semberija and to Serbia was severed, but that it was re-established in late July and 1992 after the successful completion of Operation Corridor 92. The Krajina also had an air bridge. There was an ability to get people to Banja Luka. I'm assuming that if they hadn't been able to get to Banja Luka the 16th Assembly Session wouldn't have taken place there. I believe there were helicopter flights being able to go in and out there. The airport was not -- was not put out of action, and I believe that there were flights in and out of Banja Luka. So it wasn't completely isolated, but I do take your point certainly that the road connection through the Krajina was severed for a period but that it was achieved -- reconnected after Operation Corridor and then it was expanded in -- from late July all the way through into September/October time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we next look at 65 ter 428.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It is a document that the Prosecution intended to tender alongside your report. It is 65 ter 428, page 3; page 3, item 2, "counter-intelligence information." It's probably in e-court. It is item 2. It's probably page 3 in e-court. The title should be "counter-intelligence." Yes, it is towards the bottom.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Karadzic be asked to wait for the English page to appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Certain officials of the ARK are working intensively on the creation of the so-called state of Krajina, which could have negative consequences for" -- I was asked by the interpreters to wait. Yes, item 2, counter-intelligence information: "Certain officials of the ARK are working intensively on the creation of the so-called state of Krajina, which could have negative consequences for the unity of the Serbian people in BH and the struggle they have waged." Did you have this document when you drew up your report, given the fact that it is on the OTP list?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember seeing this document, Mr. Karadzic. It may well be one that was obtained after I wrote the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have this admitted? Let's have 65 ter 432, another OTP document that they will seek to tender through you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm not objecting. I'm not sure exactly what Mr. Karadzic means when he says 65/428 is something we intended to tender alongside his report. I'm just not sure what he means. I tendered what I intended to tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. What did you mean, Mr. Karadzic, by saying that this is the document Prosecution wanted to tender?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They included this document as a reference concerning this witness. It was probably part of a more comprehensive list, but in any case it was on the list as 65 ter 428. It was supposed to be a document that should be noted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, let's proceed. I don't see this -- those items in the list of the documents to be used in his direct. We'll admit 65 ter 428.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1941, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have a look at this document. Can we go to page 3, item 3. Situation in the territory is discussed. It is stated that there was a struggle for power in the various organs of the SR BH which has an impact on the military structures. There are also parallel ministries of the Serbian Republic of BiH and the Autonomous Region of the Krajina. Did you make note of that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I'd have to go to my document footnotes, but as I said I don't -- I do make reference to the fact that there were tensions and difficulties. I think the ARK certainly, for example, wanted to have some unity with the Serb areas in Croatia and there are other issues that they may well have been in disagreement with, and I've made reference in the report that there were these tensions. But many of them seem to be internal, as they say, jockeying for influence. But I didn't see them somehow impacting on what the Krajina Corps was doing. And, in fact, General Talic was active in trying to resolve those differences by having meetings and -- there are referenced in the -- in some of his documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have this admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Exhibit D1942.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at paragraph 1.124, where you say that you were aware of the fact that local authorities in certain municipalities had the ambition of complementing their power by controlling certain military instances in the municipality. Talic, it seems, was asked to exert influence through the ARK government to exclude such extremist elements. Kljuc is mentioned specifically. You can see here that the army structures of Kljuc are asking to influence local politicians through the ARK government so as not to try to control their regional military unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It might take a bit of time to go through the documents and the reports, but my understanding of what happened was that there were tensions in Kljuc and that I think some Muslims were killed or a Muslim was killed and there was a request to Talic -- or Talic sent a request to the ARK, in essence for them to use their authority to somehow, I think, avoid misunderstandings and conflicts with the JNA in that area. I think Talic clearly indicated through that request that the ARK were of some significance and could help there. And I think there was also pressure to use the JNA unit in Kljuc, so he was trying to resolve that through the organs of authority. I believe that the same unit that was there at the beginning of the May was actually the unit that was involved in the take-over or operations, disarmament operations, at the end of May. So the same unit that they were talking about I think at the beginning of May was actually the same unit that ended up conducting those operations at the end of that month. But for me to get it exactly right, I'd have to go back to my footnotes. But clearly General Talic felt that in order to resolve whatever pressures were there, the ARK were the body that he should go to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, please conclude in three minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, this had to do with my question, whereby I said that you were obviously aware that there were autonomous streaks at municipal levels and that each administrative unit wanted to have an army of its own. In any case, you seem to have expanded on it. Look at your paragraph 2.24, where you -- it is page 69 of your report. You noted that until the VRS was established, units functioned on the principle of self-organisation. Correct? [In English] "Development" [Interpretation] You quote there. [In English] "Important development in the first period from April the 1st to the 15th of June was the self-organising of municipal and other regional units on the basis of Territorial Defence ..." and so on and so on.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the patriotic influence of the SDS, yes, it does note.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.
