Let me ask you this: Did you know that under the Tito's doctrine of an armed population, municipalities were sovereign in terms of defence and that the municipal president was the supreme commander of the forces in his territory as well as that there were municipal units in which everyone was obliged to fight whether they had or had not received orders to that effect?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of the Law on All People's Defence. I'm aware that people in a time of crisis could be mobilised into the Territorial Defence and it was the responsibility of all citizens to contribute to the defence of the state and -- but I do not believe that that had much, if any, of a bearing on the situation that I saw in the Krajina in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me this: Did you know that the ARK in the fall of 1992 was abolished and that all regional autonomies ceased to exist, since it was concluded that the central state organs did not have sufficient influence over their functioning?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware at some stage in late 1992 the ARK did cease to function. Why that happened or what negotiations went on was not part of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It was done by changing the constitution, Mr. Brown. You probably remember. Did you go through the papers we provided to you which are actually corrections and did you enter the corrections in the errata sheet presented to this Chamber, particularly because specific items were pointed out to you in previous cases, namely, these are paragraphs 1.114, 2.18, 2.24, 2.76, 1.31, 1.105, 2.5, and 2.80?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, Mr. Karadzic. I believe that was the homework that Mr. Robinson gave me over the weekend. I looked at the eight sections that were given to me, and in the point number 1 which was paragraph 1.114, I didn't believe there was a need to change any of the report. Paragraph 2.18, I didn't believe there was a requirement to change anything in the report except that there is a misidentification of an ERN number, which has not been flagged up in the two errata sheets that I produced before and I'm more than happy to add a third errata shirt in order to do that. Number 3 which was paragraph 2.24 has already been changed in errata sheet number 2. 2.76 was a reference in relation to -- I believe Mr. Ackerman highlighted that there was no attack in Celinac. I disagree with Mr. Ackerman's point. However, on looking at the actual language I used in the document, I'm more than happy to amend that to read "military operations" rather than "attack." There are two references in the report which highlight that there were operations in Celinac. And so my point, I believe, stands. I don't think Mr. Ackerman was correct to say there were no operations in Celinac, I believe there were, and there's two references in there. But I'm more than happy to provide a slight modification to the language of one of the sentences in there. In paragraph -- point number 6, which is paragraph 1.105, Ms. Loukas indicated or put the point that she believed there was a deliberate omission by me to paragraph 10 of the Crisis Staff document which related to the issues of prisoners of war. And I indicated that I was using selected issues relating to military components of the Crisis Staff, but I'm more than happy to include paragraph 10 in an errata sheet. But I don't think that it substantively changes my point about Crisis Staffs. Point number 7 which was paragraph 2.5, there was an issue about where I put the footnote reference. I put the footnote reference at the end of the sentence and there was an argument that the reference only reflected the securing of key facilities in the sentence, and the sentence itself was, I think I said, securing territories, key facilities, and other aspect. And I think that the Judge at the time said would it be more appropriate to put the footnote in the middle of the sentence on the issue of key -- securing key facilities, to which the footnote referred. Again, I don't think it's substantively changes the comment that I made, but I'm more than prepared to change the footnote rather than changing the footnote to the right part of the sentence to actually include references to the securing of territories -- in essence, to expand the footnote that I think it makes it more clear. I don't believe that it substantively changes anything in the report and I think it was maybe a rather administrative point. Point 8 which is paragraph 2.80 has already been amended in relation to the errata sheet I pushed out on the 11th of November, so it has already been included in an errata sheet. So in essence, I have looked at the documents. In two of them they have already been amended in an errata sheet, a previous errata sheet. One of them I would argue needs no change whatsoever. And the remaining five, I believe, are of a minor nature that do not necessarily require substantive changes in any of the analysis, but I'm more than happy and have already done -- provided or written up a third errata sheet putting those changes in, which I'm more than happy to submit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: At this stage we are -- probably need to admit your hallmark sheet into evidence, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it that has been disclosed to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It has, Your Honour, and there are -- no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll upload it into e-court, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll give that number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, what about 131, you skipped that one. Did you change that one also?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I changed that and -- of a minor nature and I'm happy to put it into the -- a third errata sheet. The problem with 131 was that there was one footnote reference -- there was a large quote and there actually was one footnote reference, but actually the quote comes from two documents. And in the transcript they provided one of -- the extra document but in the wrong place. So it is an administrative issue and what I've done on this new errata sheet is to clear that up. 1.31 should have two footnote references, not one, and they highlighted one of them during the transcript but didn't highlight the second one. So it doesn't substantively change the quote, but actually it's from two documents, not one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1943, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two more short questions, Mr. Brown, and I wish to inform the Trial Chamber that I haven't had time to deal with the credibility or the qualifications or other organisational matters --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, unacceptable comment. Please continue with your two last questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: First question: Do you agree, as an officer and an analyst, that it's the duty of a senior officer to notice, make note of, and report on the mistakes committed by subordinate?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a former soldier, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Second question: Your complete analysis comprises about 500 paragraphs and many footnotes. All that you have learned and put down as -- as Serbian misdeeds, have you learned all that from the documents of the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've highlighted that earlier, Mr. Karadzic. The documents I predominantly used were documents contemporaneous, 1st Krajina Corps documents, written at the time; a number of police documents also written at the time; a small number of media reports from the time, too; and one or two videos. But the overwhelming majority of the documents used in the report come from the archive of the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic. Do you have re-examination, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, then, that concludes your evidence, Mr. Brown. Thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you for your patience, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, would you suggest that we take a short break or is it okay to continue outright?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm happy to continue, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then please call your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, while we're bringing in the witness, I just want to advise the Trial Chamber yesterday the Appeals Chamber made a decision concerning delayed disclosure of Witness KDZ320 and referred the matter to the Trial Chamber and I want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, we are aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I figured you were. But I wanted to let you know that we would not be filing any further pleadings, but we ask you to take into consideration what we filed before the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we begin to hear your evidence, there is an administrative matter that I'd like to deal with. So in order to do that, we shall move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You can hear me okay?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I just want to remind you of one thing before we start, and that is that you should not use your own name, please. So don't say your own name.

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So as I indicated, Mr. Witness, you will be called -- we will refer to you as simply Witness or Witness number 39.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And the other thing I wanted to advise you, sir, I know you've had a leg injury and the past and that sometimes your leg causes you pain if you sit a long time. So please do not feel self-conscious, if you begin to be in pain and you need to stand up and walk around, please just let me know.

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: All right, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The first thing I would like to do is bring up 65 ter 90301, a pseudonym sheet. It should not be broadcast, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, sir, up on a screen is going to come a piece of paper with your name written on it. Don't read it out loud. Just look at it, please, and tell me, yes or no, is your name printed on that piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I can see my name on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we admit that under seal, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3938, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, sir, as I explained to you, as has been done before, we're not going to ask you all the same questions today about your experiences. What we're going to do is seek to put into evidence your testimony in the Popovic trial. So I'm going to ask you a couple questions about that. Number one: Do you remember that you testified in that case, the Popovic case, in 2007?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: No, I don't remember, but I'm sure I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you reviewed your testimony from that case. Do you remember --

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Yes, I did review it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When you listened to that testimony, when you testified in the Popovic case, can you confirm that when you listened to it you didn't hear any mistakes, that the testimony -- that the record was accurate?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Yes, it was accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you please tell the Trial Chamber, if you were asked the same questions again today, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: The answers to the same questions would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: With that, Your Honours, I would seek to tender 22402A under seal, which is the testimony in the Popovic case from November 1st and 2nd, 2007; as well as 22402B, which is the public transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Both versions will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 22402A will be Exhibit P3939 under seal, and 65 ter 22402B will be Exhibit P3940.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Witness, before I ask you any questions I am going to read a brief summary of your evidence and then I'll ask you some questions.

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The witness was born in a small hamlet in the municipality of Srebrenica. He grew up in Srebrenica municipality, raised his family there, and lived there until 11 July 1995. At about 5.00 p.m. that day he returned from his work gathering hay and he heard that Srebrenica had fallen. He heard from a neighbour that someone from civil protection had come and said that the old people and people with disabilities should go to the UNPROFOR base in Potocari and that the younger men, military-aged men, should try to save themselves by going through the woods. He set off for the UNPROFOR base with his wife, his daughter, his daughter-in-law, and his granddaughter, and because of his bad leg going through the hills he went on a horse. The witness and his family arrived in Potocari sometime after night had fallen and saw that there were already a lot of people there. The witness and his family spent the night of 11-12 July in the parking-lot of the Sacmara factory near the UNPROFOR base, and this parking-lot was filled with other people who had come there. The next morning on 12 July he heard that transportation to Tuzla had been organised. And as he waited, he saw Serb soldiers coming towards the factories near the UNPROFOR base and he saw that they were setting fire to haystacks as they approached. At about 2.00 p.m. the first buses and trucks arrived. He went to the main road in Potocari, where he saw barricades had been set up. And as the narrowing roadway led to waiting buses and trucks, he saw UNPROFOR soldiers lined up. And further down the witness saw Serb soldiers in camouflage uniforms lined up near the buses and trucks. He walked towards the buses and trucks with his family, hoping to get on one, but the witness testified that he did not even get close to the buses. As he tried to approach the buses with his family, a Serb soldier took him by the shoulder and told him, "Go to the left." He was separated from his family at this point. He was taken aside and ordered to join a group of other elderly men who had also been singled out previously. He saw other men continuing to be separated from their families, and he was detained with about 20 other elderly men at this time guarded by some Serb soldiers in camouflage uniforms who had rifles. These soldiers escorted the witness and the other men to an unfinished house near the main road. And as more and more prisoners arrived, they filled up the room where the witness was held so that some of the prisoners had to sit outside. At some point the witness remembers General Mladic spoke to the prisoners and told them that he needed 180 men for exchange for captured Serbs. All of the prisoners taken to this unfinished house were elderly or disabled, in similar condition to the witness at the time. Some had walking sticks. And during the four or so hours that they were held at the house, the men were not given food or water. Later that day, 12 July, as it was starting to get dark, as the witness recalls, the men were put on two buses that were filled to capacity, there was standing room only. They were driven to Bratunac, and there they were met by 10 or 15 Serb soldiers in front of an abandoned warehouse that the witness noticed was near a school they passed. He later learned that that school in Bratunac was called the Vuk Karadzic school. He and the others were taken inside the warehouse and made to sit down as the entrance was guarded. Men continued to be brought to the warehouse until about midnight and it was full. According to the witness's estimate, there were 400 men held there. They were in similar condition to him, mainly elderly men or men with disabilities. They were kept in suffocating heat, it was overcrowded, and they weren't given any food or water. When they complained, they were threatened or their complaints were actually met with violence. Throughout that night of 12 July, Serb soldiers took about 40 prisoners in total from the warehouse, calling people out. He could hear blows being struck, moaning, screaming after the men were taken outside. Some of these men were returned to the room with blood on them, and the witness remembers that five men who had been brought out and returned died during the night. The witness recalls two particular prisoners being taken out of the warehouse. The first, Ibran Mustafic, did not come back. The witness thought that Ibran Mustafic had been murdered; however, sometime later after escaping to Muslim-held territory, he subsequently learned that this man had not been killed. The second man, Hamed Efendic, was taken out. The witness heard shots and he heard somebody outside saying, "You can drag him away. He's finished. He's dead." The next morning, 13 of July, the prisoners were given water. They were allowed to remove the dead from the warehouse. The witness did not take part in this removal of the dead prisoners, but those who did when they returned described seeing a pile of bodies behind the warehouse. And also that morning, the Serb soldiers demanded that the prisoners there surrender their valuables, their money, and their personal property and their ID. During the day until they were taken away, soldiers continued calling prisoners out of the warehouse, beating and killing them. The witness himself personally witnessed one man being killed by the soldiers guarding them. He saw this prisoner being hit with an iron bar by one soldier and then saw another soldier strike the prisoners in the back with an axe. In the witness's estimate, this is during the day of the 13 July, about another 40 men were killed. And now moving to the evening of the 13th of July and the transportation to Orahovac. On the evening of the 13th of July, the witness recalls Mladic coming to the warehouse and telling the prisoners that they would be exchanged. At that time the prisoners were counted and there were 296 of them. Soon after, six buses arrived and the men, the prisoners, were told to board them. Each bus was guarded by a soldier with a rifle, automatic rifle. As far as the timing, it was light when the prisoners boarded the buses but they didn't leave right away. They stayed on the buses for some time until it was getting dark and the lights came on in Bratunac. The convoy of buses set out, the witness thinks, about 8.00 or 9.00 p.m. on 13 July as it was getting dark. It stopped at Drinjaca on the way and then continued and proceeded north through Zvornik towards Karakaj and there made a left turn and went west until they stopped at a school. He estimated that the prisoners arrived at the school sometime after midnight approximately 2.00 a.m., now the early morning hours of the 14th of July. They were met there by 10 to 15 Serb soldiers. He and the other prisoners got off the buses and entered the school's gym. No food or water was provided to them, and as more prisoners filled up the gym, the conditions worsened, it was hot, it was July, some men were forced to sit in other men's laps and it became suffocating. The soldiers guarding the prisoners kept ordering them to move back, move back to make room for more prisoners and sometimes threatened to shoot them and fired over their heads in order to herd them back. One prisoner who complained about the conditions, he was taken out. The witness heard shots and the prisoner didn't come back. According to his memory, the last of the prisoners arrived sometime around 10.00 a.m. on the morning of 14 July. The witness also remembers that at one point General Mladic arrived to the school and told them they would be taken either to Bijeljina or to Fikret Abdic, as he said. Later, the prisoners started to be blindfolded, led out of the gym, walked over a platform and were put on a small TAM truck. Each prisoner was given a drink of water from a little cup as he was blindfolded and placed on the TAM truck. When his turn came, the witness was also boarded on a truck, a small truck, which proceeded along the road for a short distance before turning off into a pasture. And after he was blindfolded, he pushed his blindfold up a little bit on his forehead. He could see that the truck was followed by an armed soldier in a car. The witness saw many bodies as the truck continued further before it ultimately stopped. And then as it continued further, he could see another group of bodies where the truck stopped. Two soldiers opened the back of the truck and the prisoner and the other men were taken off and told where to stand and to keep quiet. And the witness recalls General Mladic being present at the execution site. As soon as the truck left, the soldiers opened fire on the men standing up in the row. The witness was not hit, but he fell to the ground as other prisoners in his group who had been shot fell on and around him. As he lay still he saw the TAM truck return and another group of prisoners arrived. They were taken off, lined up in four rows, and shot. The witness saw this happening over and over again as he lay there. After it became dark, prisoners were still continuing to be brought to the site, and the executions continued under the lights provided by two excavators which had been brought there to dig graves. He continued to lie still until the last TAM truck came and left, and everyone from the gym, it seemed to him, had been killed. He called out to see if any other prisoners had survived. And only one person responded and spoke up. And together he and this other man made their escape, they walked away. In the morning they were joined by a third survivor of the same execution. These three men walked on and arrived in a safe area, a safe territory for them, about 19 July 1995, a Wednesday. That's the end of the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, I have just a few questions for you now. Okay?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you heard my summary. Without saying the name of your village, is it right that you were born and grew up in Srebrenica municipality?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Yes, I was born there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Please wait for my question to finish so that we have a clear transcript. Okay?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you were married and you had children in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Please tell the Court, why did you leave Srebrenica in July 1995? What made you leave where you'd been born and lived your whole life?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Because our local commune was shelled all day and the mosque was also pulled down. It was totally destroyed. And the minaret was demolished. There was so many shells that people were hiding in river-beds. And when it stopped in the afternoon, I went to gather hay. There were no shots to be heard. When there was the news that Srebrenica had fallen and that we had to go to the UNPROFOR base because Srebrenica would be taken by Serb soldiers and they would kill whoever would remain behind in the village. That's why we had to leave forcibly, otherwise we would be killed. A couple of elderly people stayed behind because they had nobody to escort them. They were all killed. They never made it to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Just a couple more questions now because, as I said, we're putting in your other testimony. I want to move now to the later part of what happened to you when you were held in the school after having been taken away from Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I please have 65 ter 03199 on the screen, e-court page 140. And those books have been distributed, Your Honour, in hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right, sir, please take a look at that photo in front of you and tell me if you can see it clearly.

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recognise the place in this photo? Can you tell us what we see here?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: I can see a school and this gymnasium where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And could you indicate, if you can on this photo, if you're able to, the area where the TAM trucks were parked when you were taken out of the gym to be taken to the execution site.

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Here, and this is where we entered the gymnasium. There's a door there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Could somebody please help the witness to mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, sir, if you could just draw -- wait a sec -- wait for my question.

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you could just draw a circle in the general area where you remember the trucks parking, the TAM trucks, when they came to take you away from the school.

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Uh-huh, here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. So they parked close to the door?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: There was a platform that was level with the truck 's loading surface and we didn't have to climb up. So we could walk in straight from this -- from the top of these stairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Out of the door we see there into the trucks?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: You could tell when you look at the trucks that they were empty when they arrived, and then people would get on the trucks and sit down. And it went on that way until the trucks were full. Then -- that's when they would stop loading. The other truck would set off and followed by a red car. And the one guy would stick out his automatic rifle from the passenger seat through the window and said, "Shut up, don't talk, or I'll shoot you all." The truck had a tarp all over except for the rear end where it wasn't fastened, so we were able to see the red car following us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I tender that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we ask the witness to put the date and his signature as number 39 with the assistance of our usher. Could you wait a minute.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. All right. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Witness, if you could just put 24/11/11 on there and then the number 39.

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: You mean over here? What time is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You don't need to put the time, it's okay. Just 11 for the month and 11 for the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think that's all right. And if you could just put the number 39 next to there, please.

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I tender that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3941, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honours, we will be tendering the entire book as an exhibit later, so I'm not sure even though I just said that we need to tender that page at the moment but -- oh, he's marked it, of course, so, yes, we will need to tender that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to show you another photo now, sir, same exhibit, if we could go to page 160. All right, sir, I'll ask you the same thing. Make sure you can see it clearly. Take a look at this photo and tell me if you can tell us what we see in this photo.

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: I see it clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And do you recognise this place?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: I see the way we went. Now, the railroad was up and we walked through the underpass and then we walked across the pastures. It should have been here approximately where we were unloaded and executed, here, right by the woods. The forest was behind us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, sir. And with the pen, if you could just draw an oval or a circle where you -- best you can remember you were standing at this execution site when they shot at you.

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Yes. Well, here, that's where it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And again, if you could just write the date, 24/11, in the bottom and your number, 39.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I wonder whether the witness can mark the road he walked through. Can you do that, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can, but I need some more here because I walked this way. If I look at the picture now, you see, I couldn't have crossed the pastures here because it was uphill. I could not walk uphill, so I was trying to see where it was easier to walk uphill. So that's how I went to the end of this pasture and then I started walking up. So the woods were there, I mean the forest consisted of big trees, but I was bothered by the bushes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The witness said the railroad was up and we walked through the underpass and then we walked across the pastures, so if you could clarify that. So you walked through that underpass we -- which we see in this picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Now back to you, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I would tender that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sir, could you put number 39 as well kindly, number 39.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit it as Exhibit P3942.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, sir, in your statement of 21 July 1995, just a couple days after you arrived in Bosnian-held territory, you were able to name six men who'd been on the same TAM truck with you to the execution site. If you remember the names of those six men now who you knew were on the truck with you, could you please tell them to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Jakub Mekanic, then Ljubovic Suljo then Ismet Mehmedovic, Izet, actually, then Hasib Hasanovic then Sefko Gabelic then Adil Tursunovic. There were more of them, but those were the ones who were there close to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And do you know, sir, did any of these men who you knew, did any of them survive this execution?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: None of them survived. The only one who survived out of the thousands of us that were there was I bro Mustafic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I don't have any more questions right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sir, we'll have a break for 25 minutes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- and after which you'll be further cross-examined by Mr. Radovan Karadzic. But before we do that, I take it there are several associated exhibits to be tendered?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: They will be all admitted and given a number in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll take a break for 25 minutes and resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we begin, Mr. Witness, sir, when you answer the questions put by Mr. Karadzic, please put a pause before you start answering the question because both of you are speaking the same language. So we have -- in order for the answer to be correctly interpreted, please wait for a moment. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, that was an example of how things should not be done. You should wait for the interpretation of my words to finish.

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that two days after you got out into the territory of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina you gave one statement, and then four days after that yet another statement in Zivinice and in Tuzla; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: I don't remember, but I did give statements, I did. I don't remember where or when.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have to wait for your words to be interpreted as well, so you have to understand that that is why I pause. However, when you gave these statements you signed both of them; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you a soldier of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, in your first statement given on the 21st of July you said that you were a civilian and that you were not engaged in a military way and you said that you weren't armed either; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: I was not armed. I did not have any clothes but my own and I worked by the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, in Tuzla four days later, or rather, on the 22nd of July, you gave a statement in which you said that you were a member of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina up until the demilitarisation of Srebrenica, when you handed over your weapons; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: I don't know what was written there. I don't know when they handed over the weapons and when demilitarisation took place, but then until then I was by this kitchen. So then when this kitchen was disbanded, I was no longer there because there was no kitchen there any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is this unit that had this kitchen that you were attached to? If you think that this could identify you, we can move into private session. Would you like to go into private session or can you tell us what unit this was where you worked at this kitchen?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: I don't know what the name of this unit was, but it was in Suceska, the unit that was there, that's the unit that I was attached to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was that the 283rd or 284th?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: I really would not know. If that's the way it was, well then yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was Zulfo Tursunovic the commander of that unit?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's it. Zulfo Tursunovic was there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that Zulfo Tursunovic had completed only four years of elementary school education?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: That I could not tell you because I really do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was anybody else from your family one of his soldiers?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Yes, for a while my son and then he went on to become a teacher at school. When the school started he was a teacher at the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where were you carrying out combat operations, that unit, where?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: We only defended ourselves in Suceska. I don't know that any combat operations took place anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please don't mention the name of your hamlet because Suceska is a local commune; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How far away is Suceska from the town itself, the small town of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Say 14 or 15 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As you take the road, right, there is a road there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Yes, yes, there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does this road go on, does it go somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: It goes on towards Derventa-Milici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there a line of separation there or a front line?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which brigade was facing you on the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Well, that I don't know. That's what you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could it be the Milicka Brigade?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Milici were the closest there, but what their name was I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that line was there until April or March 1993; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: I don't know for how long it was there, but it was there until the demilitarisation and afterwards it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, there was still some demarcation facing the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Well, just observing, sort of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Observing, facing the Milici Brigade, well, then if there were only observers there then it was easy for the Milici Brigade to walk in; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: There was UNPROFOR; they were protecting us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that Zulfo Tursunovic in 1995 was Naser Oric's deputy and that Naser Oric was the commander of the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Now, was he his deputy, I don't know. Naser Oric was the commander, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how many brigades were there in that division, five brigades and one independent battalion; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: That I don't know because I didn't go there and I don't know what was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was Zulfo Tursunovic like in terms of his nature? How did he treat Serbs?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Go to Milici and ask them how he treated them that night in 1992 when they were taken prisoner, and you know that full well. They were taken prisoner and they were treated like gentlemen and they were given meat and they were drinking and also they were swearing at your soldiers, what they did to their neighbours, and they said, "We were treated like gentlemen at Zulfo's."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you mentioned demilitarisation. Did that actually happen when Srebrenica became a protected area and was it truly demilitarised?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Well, that's what people say, that it was. I did not go out there to demilitarise it and I didn't really care about that kind of thing. You should really put that question to someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's the way it's going to be. At the time of demilitarisation, that was the so-called 8th Operative Group and after demilitarisation was turned into the 28th Division; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: I don't know about that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Now we get to these critical events. You say - and you said that today as well during this examination-in-chief - that someone came and said to you that Srebrenica had fallen or that it will fall and that those who are not combatants should go to Potocari; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They said that Srebrenica had fallen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I see. Thank you. So could you then get to Potocari without going through Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Yes. Because I took this other road. I did not walk along the road. I went over the hills.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was that longer?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: That was closer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how far away was the line of separation from your village and from your hamlet?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: There was just this brook that separated us, and I didn't really measure the distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see Serb soldiers on the other side of the brook?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Of course I did. I saw as many as you want in the hills. They had three tanks, one howitzer, and a few launchers. We saw that they had that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Aha. And you saw them -- well, I'm not talking about July now, you saw them from the demilitarisation up until 1995 you saw them there; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: I don't know about afterwards, how many of them were there, and where they were, I cannot say. I didn't really ask anyone whether there was anyone out there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, you say that when you went there you saw that haystacks were on fire. Whose haystacks were they?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Muslim haystacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was that used for?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Perhaps you can tell us that. I wouldn't know. It's a question for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Not the burning of haystacks, Witness, but what was the hay used for?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: For cattle, of course. I was -- I thought you were asking me about why you burnt them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So the population there are mostly farmers?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have cattle?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What did you have, what kind of animals?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Is it really necessary for me to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If you please.

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Two cows, about 20 sheep, and a horse.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about the other people in the hamlet?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Some had more, some had less.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But there wasn't a single household that did not have some farm animals; correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So the haystacks were set on fire just before the reaping season; therefore, the old hay was burned?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: No, it was the newly harvested hay. And even the wheat had been reaped.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Wheat, I see. What kind of plants do you have there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Corn, wheat, fruit, and tobacco.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tobacco?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. That was for your use, but did you have any surplus? Did you sell it?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Sell what, hay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, farm produce, milk, cheese, lamb, wheat, corn?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: I didn't sell anything. We barely had enough for ourselves, for the family.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there people who produced more and what did they do with it?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: All refugees who came from the municipalities of Vlasenica and Han Pijesak were there to be fed. We distributed it all. Nothing was sold. I think there were refugees from five municipalities, including Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then you say you saw many people in Potocari. And as you said today and previously, you were taken to a building with some 40 or 50 men; correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say that on the 12th -- did you arrive on the 12th or on the evening of the 11th?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: The evening of the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On Wednesday, the 12th, the building was visited by General Mladic; correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say in one of the statements that he walked in, introduced himself, he greeted you as neighbours, he said that you knew who he was, and then he asked you what were you going to do with Alija. And he suggested that you join Fikret Abdic; correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber who Fikret Abdic is, aka Babo?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Fikret Abdic was in Velika Kladusa. I don't know what he was, a manager in Agrokomerc. After that I don't know what his position was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me assist you. Was he a Muslim champion? Was he not in the Presidency and received the most votes?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: That is correct and he handed over power to Alija. He actually won the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You concluded that Mladic was in favour of you joining Abdic rather than Izetbegovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also say that he was pleasant in the way he addressed you, that he seemed to be mild in character, and that you could trust him?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: When we asked him about the situation, he said that some 180 Serbs were held prisoner in Tuzla and that he had to take us prisoner in order to have us exchanged for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What sort of clothes was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Camouflage fatigue with rank designation without a cap.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where could you see his rank?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: On his shoulder or upper arm or maybe both. I don't know. But I know we could see his rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At what time did General Mladic walk into the house on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: I can't be certain. Perhaps at around 6.00 or 7.00, maybe two hours before it got dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And he didn't stay there long, did he?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: No, he did not. He took the same way back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Next you were taken from there to Bratunac. I was confused a little by Mr. Nicholls' interpretation of what you said. You seem to have said that you were transferred onboard two trucks that were packed. How many of you were there and how many fitted on one truck?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: We were not on any trucks, we were on buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What size buses?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Regular buses. I didn't measure their length. There must have been at least 70 of us in any given bus. They were packed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So it has nothing to do with the 40 or 50 people in the house but there were other people too; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: In the -- on the ground level of the house there were as many people as there could be and the extra people had to sit around the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: They were seated; correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: They were sitting around the house. I'm not sure the interpreters managed to understand our local dialect, but am I correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Yes, they were seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Next you were taken to Bratunac. Where to?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Close to the bus station in Bratunac, and there they took a right turn where you go to Kravica. We passed by a school and a warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you then put in the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So it wasn't a school?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: It was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that in Tuzla you were explained what the building was?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Yes. Some people from Bratunac whom I came across in Tuzla, they explained it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In Tuzla you were also explained where the place of the execution was and the fence was described to you as well as the underpass under the railroad?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Yes, and the gym where some played basketball.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who described it to you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: I can't remember them, some Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were they taken there too so that they knew where you had been?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: No. I told you that in peace time they used to play basketball there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did they describe it to you before the 21st of July when you provided your statement or was it only after you had given your statement?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Well, I can't say that with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the size of the first warehouse where you were put in?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: In Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: I couldn't say. I think some 400 of us were inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Four hundred. But how sizeable was the warehouse when all of you could be inside?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: I really can't say. If you don't know, I don't either. Perhaps I did know back then, but I can no longer say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'm confused a bit. You were told that it was a warehouse belonging to a co-operative, so what does the Vuk Karadzic school have to do with anything?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: The school is away from the warehouse. It is not close. We passed by the school. When I was asked where we had gone, I told them we passed by a school and there was a warehouse of the school there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In Tuzla they told you it was a co-operative's warehouse; correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Yes. There was a co-operative warehouse in Kravica as well, where many of the killings took place, and they gave up the Bratunac warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you were not held in the Vuk Karadzic school?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say that in the warehouse there were 400 of you guarded by two soldiers; correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Not two. That evening there were more. When one issued orders he said that 12 of you should do as ordered, is it clear, and they all said in unison "clear." And that's when they started taking us out and killing us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Excuse me, just from now on I'm going to ask for cites, if possible, when it's "you said" or "in your statement," this or that, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I understood correctly, my esteemed colleague Mr. Nicholls himself said in the summary that the witness was held in the Vuk Karadzic school. I can even provide you a line reference. It is between lines 58 and 68 -- sorry, pages. How high were the walls of the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Perhaps around 4 metres. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said, did you not, that on the wall there was a window with glass panes; correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Yes, just under the ceiling, under the roof.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you weren't able to see anything through it because it was far too high up; correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just make it clear, I don't think Mr. Nicholls said he was in the Vuk Karadzic school.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That was what my point was going to be, Your Honour, if you look at what I said. I said: "They were driven to Bratunac and there they were met by 10 or 15 Serb soldiers in front of an abandoned warehouse that the witness noticed was near a school they passed ..." and then I continued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He later learned the school in Bratunac was called the Vuk Karadzic school.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, I also said at line 13: "Men continued to be brought to the warehouse until about midnight when it was full."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, but in any event --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apologies. I seem to have noticed the reference to the Vuk Karadzic school because it seemed important to me to point out that he was not held there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you counted in the warehouse and how many times?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Once only.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Yes, the next day in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then they counted around 400 of you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: 296 people who were alive at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay, I'm -- I don't mean to object, but he has to be fair in putting the questions to the witness. The witness -- I don't know where he's getting the point that the witness said or that there were 400 people counted in the next day. And the way the question is phrased, it sounds to the witness as though it's something he has said, that they were counted -- 400 people the next day.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps Mr. Robinson could tell us. I believe it was one page before where the witness said that there were around 400.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Didn't you say a moment ago that some 400 people were taken to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Yes, when I said that I supposed that that was the total. There were many killed in one night - I think 14 - and then ten of them were taken the next morning to load the dead bodies and they didn't return either. And it continued. In my assessment, some 40 were killed that way. The next day, just before it got dark, another ten were taken to load the bodies; they didn't return either. And that's when I say that 296 remained, but I believe the initial figure must have been at around 400.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. It's no point, but, Mr. Nicholls, it was you that summarised it like this. According to the witness's estimate, there were 400 men held there, it's line 15, page 5 --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. But when the -- when they were counted the next day, it's a -- the different number that the witness just quoted us. So he estimated that there were 400 that arrived there and then when they were put on the buses to be taken away there was 296, if I remember the number the witness said was counted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think you summarised -- you referred to 296 in your summary. So let's continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which killings did you see? You saw one killing in the gym; correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Which gym? In Karakaj?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I understood that someone was killed with a metal bar and then an axe in the gym?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Yes, I did see that. In the morning, they allowed us to use a toilet which was in a side room. There was a hall and there was then a small room to the left. As we went to the toilet, they would simply put a hand on the person's shoulder and kill them later. We weren't supposed to -- allowed to look. As I was going back I saw a man being stopped that way and he was told, "Come this way." He went through them and there were three on one side and three on the other. There was another one with an automatic rifle facing the man approaching him, and he called him, "Come to me, come to me." The man did and then there was a man on the left who hit him on the back with a metal bar or perhaps on the head. And the man fell down. Another man on the right side had an axe and that axe was constantly bloody and he was showing it off to show us what he was doing. He hit him with the axe on the back. I left and the last thing I saw was that he was holding onto the axe. He either didn't want to remove it or couldn't take it out any longer. In any case, I returned to the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So that's the murder you saw. Did you see any others?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: I heard, I heard people say, "He's dead, take him away." That's what I could hear. And I could also hear when they slit their throats you could hear the gurgling sound and people being dragged across the concrete floor. That's when we knew someone had been killed. I didn't see it but I could hear the blows and noises.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Uh-huh. And you also heard when Ibro Mustafic was taken out and you concluded that he was dead?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Ibran Mustafic, here's what I stated, when he was taken out we heard noise. There was somebody with him who started shouting, and then there was silence. And then they asked, "What do you think happened to Mustafic?" And whatever happened to the others probably happened to him as well. It must have been a blow with some blunt object because we couldn't hear a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you remember, don't you, that the Muslims had tried to commit to -- had tried to -- had made two attempts on Mustafic's life and a month and a half before the fighting around Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: I don't know that. Ask Ibran about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ibran was taken out as well, but Ibran survived and after that wrote the book "A Planned Chaos" about the events in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But until they told you that he was alive, you were certain that he had been taken out and killed; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's what I said because I knew about all the others in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to know why you state in your statement that in Zivinice two days after your release, which is 65 ter 22369, page 2, and the statement that was made four days later, 65 ter 22398, nowhere do you mention that axe, which is a very graphic detail.

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: I think that I mentioned it in each of my statements. I don't remember not mentioning it. Whoever asked me if I saw a killing - and you asked me too - I always mentioned it. So whoever asked me whether I had seen any killings and I always answered, "Yes, that's the killing that I saw." And that I heard somebody being killed with a fire-arm, but only once; it wasn't used again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But did you see anybody being hit when the shot was fired?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: No, I didn't see, but I did hear the shot and I heard them say, "He's dead. Take him to the heap."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we can check whether the axe is mentioned in those two statements, but tell me why the man was hit by the bar?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: When we arrived one of them held this bar. It was a -- it has a -- had a square section, and he held the bar and threatened us, "Here's what you will be killed with tonight." And the same axe was held by another and he threatened us. He also had a knife and said, "This is what I'll use to cut your throats."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, but why was he hit?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: You ask the one who hit him why, because he was a Bosniak, a Muslim; that's the only reason why.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But didn't you say in your statement in Tuzla that they found a knife on him and that the soldier hit him, as you say, with a metal bar, killing him instantly, but you never mention another soldier or an axe. So is it true what you stated, that they found a concealed knife on his person?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: They asked one man, "What do you have?" And they hit him right there on the spot and he died of it. You want us to go into the details? When they discovered that he was making some things -- he was making pulleys and he had a knife on him and they found it and that's when it happens -- happened. But I didn't see what happened because I was at the toilet, but I saw him taken -- being taken out to the yard and there he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you stated that they found a knife on his person and that's why he was hit with a bar?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: No. That wasn't it. I didn't see who it was or what happened, but they took him by the shoulder and pulled him away. And another was asked by the door, "What's in your bag? Take it out." And they found a knife in that bag that he had used to make pulleys, but they immediately dragged him out and killed him outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, if there's time on Monday we'll check that on the relevant pages, but you stated that there was no beating before 10.00 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Until 10.00 p.m., people were still being brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But who stayed behind with you after 10.00 p.m.? Some soldiers and officers had left and somebody stayed.

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: I don't know who they were. They were some guys at the door where the battery or torch is. There were around five or six.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So after 10.00 p.m. some people with torches turned up. Is it true that they were looking for specific persons?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: They only asked who was from where. They were asking whether there was anybody from beyond village so and so, and nobody responded. And then they would shine their torches on somebody and that person had to leave. They asked no more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which villages did they take interest in?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Glogova, Hranca, and Voljavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know why they were doing that, whether they had some old misgivings, or whether there had been fighting and that people from those villages had been going to Serbian villages, Kravica and others, to kill the locals?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: That's not true. Glogova and Hranca fell first and the Serbian soldiers took Glogova and Hranca first. The people fled to the forests and watched their villages burn. And in Bratunac there still -- there was nothing happening still.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that on Christmas day according to the Orthodox calendar, quite -- 1993 there was a Muslim attack and 54 civilians were killed?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: But why didn't you let humanitarian aid pass? That case nobody would have attacked Kravica. People were hungry, their children were starving, and that's when -- when they went to raid those places, because they didn't want their children to die of hunger. People were saying, "I don't care if I get killed. I can't watch my child dying of hunger." And you didn't let humanitarian aid pass through. You're the one who's guilty for Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Never mind that. We'll see -- we'll clarify that with the Trial Chamber, but how many Muslims were killed in Kravica on Christmas day 1993?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Not one, sir. 34 Serbian civilians got killed.

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: I don't know about that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. They were looking for people from certain villages, right, and taking them out; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: No, they first looked for certain persons, but nobody responded. And later on they know -- they didn't ask anymore, "Where are you from?" But instead, they would shine their torches on someone and the one would have to come out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Oh, now I understand. They used their torches and whoever they pointed their torch at had to come out?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say on the 13th of July around 6.00 p.m. Mladic came again?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How was he dressed then?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: The same way as on the previous day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The same rank insignia?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Yes, everything was the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were the rank insignia on his shoulders or the sleeves?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you anybody -- did you inform anybody what some people had done to you on the previous night?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Of course we did. Why -- we said, "Why didn't you -- or why did you do all these things to us?" So many people got killed. We almost suffocated. But nobody wanted to hear about it. They only said, "Now we're taking you to Kalesija to be exchanged."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Just a second. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No objection. I'm just concerned about the transcript because the interpreter is speaking very fast. I can hear the answers coming while the interpreter is still interpreting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could both of you slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, all right. I'll slow down. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, if you have this written text before you, when you see the cursor stop, then you can start replying, and I also have to remind myself of that.

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know who these people were who at night or during that night came to see you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Serbian soldiers, right? Or the ones who were -- who had been brought in?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The ones who asked questions, who shone their lights on you, the ones who beat people, did they introduce themselves to you? Did you find out who they were?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: No, I didn't know who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, in one of your statements, 1D4875, could we please display it, but let's not broadcast it publicly, you say that they were Black Wolves or some-such; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: I may have said that. If I did say it, then they were. At this moment, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says here on page 2 - can we see page 2 - and don't broadcast it at all, in the centre paragraph I'll read in English but you will hear the interpretation. [In English] "More Serbs arrived with torches. They asked: 'Who is from Glogova? Who is from Bratunac? Who is from Valjevo (in Serbia)? Who is from Loznica? Who is from Sabac? ' The people from Glogova put their hands up. Then the people from Bratunac, et cetera. The Serbs then said that they are 'Black Wolves' (... special military unit). They may have said that they were 'Wolves from the Drina' (another Serb special unit). I don't remember if they said 'Black Wolves' or 'Wolves from the Drina.' They were definitely one or the other." [Interpretation] So some new people arrived who had not taken you there and who hadn't been there during the day; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: At Potocari I was saying who introduced themselves to us and who approached the house. They introduced themselves as being from Uzice, others from Valjevo, others again from Novi Sad. At Bratunac, though, I cannot remember how they introduced themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In two or three lines back. [In English] "Only two Serbs stayed in the warehouse ..." [Interpretation] So there were two Serbs who stayed behind in the warehouse and there were around 350 of you; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: That is not my statement, that only two Serbs stayed in the warehouse. I don't know how many they were, but at least six of them were at the door and we saw them and there may have been more, but there were at least six of them all night long.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you notice any difference between the ones who brought you there during the day and the ones who arrived at night? If so, what kind of difference, uniform, behaviour?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Only one brought us. He was sitting next to the driver on the bus. He had an automatic rifle and I think he wore a camouflage uniform, but it was a uniform, I'm sure. And that's all. Only the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And on the bus there were about 70 Muslims and one Serb; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you say that nobody dared complain to Mladic about the beatings?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Not just one. We all cried out, "Why are you stifling us here? Why are you killing us? Why are you taking us away?" But he wouldn't even discuss it. He just said, "Now you're going to Kalesija to be exchanged."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us see what you say in your statement. Mladic mentioned some detained Serbs in Tuzla to you, right, and that there is to be an exchange?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And in your statement given to the Prosecution, 228397 [as interpreted] , on page 7, paragraph 22, you say that there were only two soldiers. How were these two soldiers dressed?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Are you asking me about Bratunac or where?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we get this document 22397 on the 65 ter list. Can we have page 5, paragraph 4. Don't have this broadcast. Is this your statement?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Yes, my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Page 5, paragraph 4, please take a look at this. This is what you say, you're speaking about Mladic: "Around 1800 hours," can this be zoomed in, "the soldiers at the door said General Mladic is coming ..." and now we're going to see what happened to you. Soon after that Mladic arrived and you described what he was wearing: He stayed by the door with the guards and we asked why we were being kept there. No one dared complain about the killings and the beatings. So Mladic had not been informed; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Well, it's not that there was one person complaining. As a group, we were saying, "Why are you killing us here? Why won't you give us water, anything?" And he said, "If there could have been an exchange sooner, this wouldn't have happened. You can count how many of you are there." He didn't even want to hear what we were saying. And he said, "Now I'm going to say how you're going to be transported to Kalesija, all of you."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Something similar is written here as well, but you say that you asked why you were being kept and then there is a sentence here that says: "No one dared to complain about the killings and beatings."

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: Not individually because otherwise such a person would have been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then you said after that that during the transport, during the transport, a red vehicle escorted the buses and that Mladic was in the red vehicle; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: In front of the factory, the battery factory, when we're going from Potocari to Bratunac, then Mladic walked up to the first bus. I was in the first bus. I was close to the driver because I was one of the last to board. And he said, "Follow the red car and go behind it." A Serb soldier came in and stood by the driver. He had an automatic rifle. He closed the door. Mladic remained on the road and we saw this red car in front of us. The red car set out and we followed the red car. We asked the driver, "Where are we going now?" And he said, "Did you hear what Mladic said, that I should follow the red car. If you know, then I know too. I have no idea where we're going. I'm just going to follow the red car." And that is how the red car went to Bratunac, turned left to Kravica, and then it turned right before the bus station and then to some school and then in front of this co-operative warehouse. The car stopped. The buses stopped. There was Serb soldiers there. There was a group there, perhaps about 15 soldiers. They said to us, "Get out." They opened the door. They said, "Get out, go into the warehouse," and that is how we got out and walked into this warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You're talking about the time when you arrived in Bratunac. I am asking you how things were when you left Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: As I was leaving Bratunac, or rather, that whereas in Bratunac, I boarded a bus. On the left-hand side Mladic was standing there. There was a group of perhaps 15 soldiers. And now I was watching for the bus. He was doing this with his hand talking to them. They were watching him, and he was saying something to them and then he left. And then we asked the driver, "What are we waiting for? Why are we not leaving?" And he said, "I don't know either. I am watching the bus in front of me, and when that bus leaves, I'll start too." And that's how we waited until the lights were turned on in Bratunac. When the lights were turned on, then the buses left and that's how we got to Drinjaca. We stopped at Drinjaca and then we continued our journey.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So around 9.30 you arrived in this school; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039
utterances.text: I think around 2.00, I think, I'm not sure, but it must have been after midnight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I think you have more, so we have to continue on Monday. It's time to conclude for the day, Mr. Witness. We --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are -- probably you will be aware of this, but you are not supposed to discuss about your testimony with anybody else. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand that. I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Pleased have a nice weekend.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I wish you the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll resume on Monday at quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
